title: Theorem

\(\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(D)\leqslant19683/5740<3.430\).

label: thm:complexity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:complexity}
For every fixed \(1\leqslant\rho<72/71\), approximating the fractional majority coloring number within multiplicative ratio \(\rho\) is NP-hard. For every fixed \(0<\delta<3/142\), computing an upper estimate with additive error at most \(\delta\) is NP-hard. Both statements hold for acyclic oriented digraphs of maximum outdegree two.
head: environment

label: lem:distribution
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:distribution}
If a random majority-stable set \(S\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(v\in S)\geqslant p>0\) for every vertex, then \(\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(D)\leqslant1/p\). Moreover, for every \(K\geqslant1\), the inequality \(\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(D)\leqslant K\) holds if and only if there is a random majority-stable set \(S\) satisfying \(\mathbb P(v\in S)=1/K\) for every vertex.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first assertion, give each majority-stable set \(I\) weight \(\mathbb P(S=I)/p\). The total weight is \(1/p\), and the weight covering a vertex \(v\) is \(\mathbb P(v\in S)/p\geqslant1\). This also proves the reverse implication in the second assertion by taking \(p=1/K\).

Conversely, take a fractional coloring of total weight at most \(K\), add any missing weight to the empty set, and divide all weights by \(K\). This gives a random majority-stable set \(S'\) with marginal \(p_v=\mathbb P(v\in S')\geqslant1/K\) at each vertex. Conditional on \(S'\), retain each \(v\in S'\) independently with probability \(1/(Kp_v)\), which belongs to \((0,1]\). The resulting subset \(S\) is majority-stable: removing vertices cannot increase the number of selected outneighbors of a remaining vertex. Finally, \(\mathbb P(v\in S)=p_v/(Kp_v)=1/K\), as required.

label: lem:pairtail
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use induction on \(r\), proving the assertion for every nonnegative \(s\). When \(r=0\), the two sides are equal.

Suppose \(r\geqslant1\). Write \(Z=W+Q\), where \(Q\sim\operatorname{Bin}(1,2b)\), \(W=I+J\), \(I\sim\operatorname{Bin}(r-1,2b)\), and \(J\sim\operatorname{Bin}(s,b)\), with these variables independent. Let \(Q'\sim\operatorname{Bin}(2,b)\) also be independent of \(W\). We first show that replacing \(Q\) by \(Q'\) cannot decrease the tail at \(t\).

For a fixed value \(w\) of \(W\), independence gives conditional tail probabilities \(\mathbb P(Q\geqslant t-w)\) and \(\mathbb P(Q'\geqslant t-w)\). If \(w\geqslant t\), both sums already reach \(t\), so both probabilities are one. If \(w\leqslant t-3\), then \(w+Q\leqslant w+2\leqslant t-1\) and \(w+Q'\leqslant w+2\leqslant t-1\), so neither sum reaches \(t\) and both probabilities are zero. Only \(w=t-1\) and \(w=t-2\) can contribute to the difference. At \(w=t-1\), the difference is \(2b-[1-(1-b)^2]=b^2\); at \(w=t-2\), it is \(0-b^2=-b^2\). Averaging these conditional differences over \(W\), each with weight \(\mathbb P(W=w)\), therefore gives
\[
\mathbb P(W+Q\geqslant t)-\mathbb P(W+Q'\geqslant t)
=b^2\bigl(\mathbb P(W=t-1)-\mathbb P(W=t-2)\bigr).
\]
To determine the sign, condition on \(I=i\), where \(0\leqslant i\leqslant r-1\), and put \(j=t-1-i\). Since \(t>r+s/2\), we have \(j\geqslant t-r>s/2\). For \(1\leqslant j\leqslant s\), the binomial mass formula gives
\[
\frac{\mathbb P(J=j)}{\mathbb P(J=j-1)}
=\frac{s-j+1}{j}\frac{b}{1-b}\leqslant1.
\]
Indeed, the integer inequality \(j>s/2\) implies \(s-j+1\leqslant j\), and \(b\leqslant1/2\) implies \(b/(1-b)\leqslant1\). If \(j=s+1\), the numerator is zero; if \(j>s+1\), both masses are zero. This also covers \(s=0\), since then \(j\geqslant1\). In every case \(\mathbb P(J=j)\leqslant\mathbb P(J=j-1)\). Multiplying these inequalities by \(\mathbb P(I=i)\) and summing over \(i\) yields \(\mathbb P(W=t-1)\leqslant\mathbb P(W=t-2)\). Substituting this inequality into the tail difference gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(W+Q\geqslant t)-\mathbb P(W+Q'\geqslant t)
&=b^2\mathbb P(W=t-1)-b^2\mathbb P(W=t-2)\\
&\leqslant b^2\mathbb P(W=t-2)-b^2\mathbb P(W=t-2)=0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, \(W+Q'\) is the sum of independent variables with laws \(\operatorname{Bin}(r-1,2b)\) and \(\operatorname{Bin}(s+2,b)\). Since \(2(r-1)+(s+2)=n\), the same threshold satisfies the induction hypothesis. Hence \(\mathbb P(Z\geqslant t)\leqslant\mathbb P(W+Q'\geqslant t)\leqslant\mathbb P(\operatorname{Bin}(n,b)\geqslant t)\), as required.

label: lem:binomial
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(2j+1,b)\), and let \(B_1,B_2\sim\operatorname{Bin}(1,b)\), all independently. Then \(Y+B_1+B_2\sim\operatorname{Bin}(2j+3,b)\). The events defining the two tails are \(A=\{Y\geqslant j+1\}\) and \(A'=\{Y+B_1+B_2\geqslant j+2\}\).

The event \(A\setminus A'\) occurs precisely when \(Y=j+1\) and \(B_1=B_2=0\). Indeed, any larger value of \(Y\), or either new success, reaches the new threshold. Conversely, \(A'\setminus A\) occurs precisely when \(Y=j\) and \(B_1=B_2=1\): a smaller value of \(Y\) cannot reach \(j+2\) with only two additional trials. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{2j+1}(b)-\Phi_{2j+3}(b)
&=\mathbb P(Y=j+1)(1-b)^2-\mathbb P(Y=j)b^2\\
&=\binom{2j+1}{j+1}b^{j+1}(1-b)^{j+2}
-\binom{2j+1}{j}b^{j+2}(1-b)^{j+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The binomial coefficients are equal, and factoring proves~\eqref{eq:binomialdifference}. Its right-hand side is nonnegative for \(b\leqslant1/2\), so the odd tails are nonincreasing and bounded by \(\Phi_1(b)=b\).

For even degree \(2j\), with \(j\geqslant1\), take independent \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bin}(2j,b)\) and \(B\sim\operatorname{Bin}(1,b)\). The event \(Y\geqslant j+1\) is contained in \(Y+B\geqslant j+1\). The latter is exactly the strict-majority event for \(2j+1\) trials. Therefore \(\Phi_{2j}(b)\leqslant\Phi_{2j+1}(b)\leqslant b\), completing the proof.

label: lem:survival
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Survival under random matchings

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a matching configuration \(M\). The vertex \(v\) is selected with probability \(b\). Conditional on its selection, its mate, if any, is absent, while all other blocks retain their independent sampling distributions. Put \(n=d-1\) if \(M\) protects \(v\), and \(n=d\) otherwise. By Section~\ref{sec:paircomparison}, the selected count among the remaining outneighbors is the sum of independent variables with laws \(\operatorname{Bin}(r,2b)\) and \(\operatorname{Bin}(s,b)\), where \(2r+s=n\). Since the deletion threshold \(\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1\) is strictly greater than \(n/2\), Lemma~\ref{lem:pairtail} gives
\[
\mathbb P(v\in S_0\mid\mathcal M=M)
\geqslant b\,\mathbb P\bigl(\operatorname{Bin}(n,b)\leqslant\lfloor d/2\rfloor\bigr).
\]
Averaging over \(M\) proves the stated bound. Removing one independent Bernoulli trial cannot decrease the probability of being at most a fixed threshold, so \(L_{d,b}(q)\) is nondecreasing in \(q\). Majority stability and the assertion for sinks follow directly from the definition of \(S_0\).

label: lem:degreemin
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For \(q=1/3\), the final bracket in~\eqref{eq:recurrence} is \((29j-26)/3\). It is negative at \(j=0\) and positive for every \(j\geqslant1\). Thus the odd-degree values decrease from degree one to degree three and increase thereafter. The even-degree comparison shows that the minimum over all positive degrees is attained at degree three.

To evaluate it, \(\Phi_3(b)=3b^2(1-b)+b^3=3b^2-2b^3\) and \(R_1=2b(1-b)\). Substitution into~\eqref{eq:Lodd} gives
\[
L_3(1/3)=b(1-\Phi_3(b))+\frac{b^2R_1}{3}
=b-\frac73b^3+\frac43b^4
=\frac{5740}{19683},
\]
where the last equality uses \(b=4/9\).

label: eq:universalconstant
title: Proof
body_md:
Use the construction of Section~\ref{sec:sampling} with \(b=4/9\). Lemma~\ref{lem:survival} and the degree estimates above give the survival guarantees
\[
p_R=\frac{20}{81},\qquad p_C=\frac{5740}{19683},\qquad
p_C-p_R=\frac{880}{19683}>0.
\]
The mixture~\eqref{eq:mixture} therefore applies. It uses \(S_0\) with probability \(\lambda=19683/21443\), and gives every vertex inclusion probability at least
\[
p=\lambda p_C=\frac{5740}{21443}=\frac{140}{523}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:distribution},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:universalconstant}
\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(D)\leqslant U:=\frac{1+2(p_C-p_R)}{p_C}=\frac{523}{140}<3.736.
\end{equation}
If \(C\) is empty or \(R\) is empty, the same mixture remains valid, though in those cases a more efficient distribution is available.

label: prop:lower
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:lower}
If \(v\) has positive outdegree \(d\), then \(\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(D)\geqslant2-\lfloor d/2\rfloor/d\geqslant3/2\). In particular, every digraph containing an arc has value at least \(3/2\), and the inequality is strict if some vertex has positive odd outdegree.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Put \(k=\lfloor d/2\rfloor\). Give \(v\) weight \((d-k)/d\), each of its \(d\) outneighbors weight \(1/d\), and every other vertex weight zero. These vertices are distinct because there are no loops. A majority-stable set omitting \(v\) has weight at most one. A set containing \(v\) contains at most \(k\) of its outneighbors, so its weight is at most \((d-k)/d+k/d=1\). The weighting is dual feasible and has total weight \(2-k/d\). Weak duality proves the claim.

label: prop:D2
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(a\) satisfy every constraint. For each \(t\in\mathbb Z_3\), form a set \(J_t\) of vertices omitted from \(S_t=V(D_2)\setminus J_t\) as follows. From each variable triple omit exactly \(x_{v,a(v)+t}\). For a constraint \(e=(u,v,c_e)\), the two labels \(a(u)+t\) and \(a(v)+c_e+t\) are distinct because \(a\) satisfies \(e\). Let \(h_e(t)\) be the unique third label, and omit exactly \(z_{e,h_e(t)}\) from its auxiliary triple. These are all the vertices of \(J_t\). Figure~\ref{fig:constraint} illustrates the construction for one constraint and \(t=0\).

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.60\linewidth]{constraint_reduction.pdf}
\caption{The digraph for two variables \(u,v\) and one constraint \(e=(u,v,1)\). The assignment \(a(u)=a(v)=1\) satisfies the constraint. For \(t=0\), the two labels used in the proof are \(a(u)=1\) and \(a(v)+1=2\), so \(h_e(0)=0\). The shaded, double-bordered vertices form \(J_0=\{x_{u,1},x_{v,1},z_{e,0}\}\); the white vertices form \(S_0\). Each white vertex of positive outdegree has exactly one shaded and one white outneighbor.}
\label{fig:constraint}
\end{figure}

We check majority stability at every type of vertex in \(S_t\). If a variable center \(x_{v,0}\) is selected, the omitted vertex of its triple is one of its two leaves. Exactly one of its two outneighbors is therefore selected. For a selected auxiliary vertex \(z_{e,i}\), we have \(i\ne h_e(t)\), so \(i\) equals exactly one of \(a(u)+t\) and \(a(v)+c_e+t\). The first equality says that \(x_{u,i}\) is omitted, and the second says that \(x_{v,i-c_e}\) is omitted. Exactly one of its two outneighbors is consequently selected. All other selected vertices are sinks. Hence \(S_t\) is majority-stable.

As \(t\) runs through \(\mathbb Z_3\), each variable vertex is omitted exactly once. Translation permutes the three labels, so \(h_e(t)=h_e(0)+t\); each auxiliary vertex is also omitted exactly once. Every vertex belongs to exactly two of \(S_0,S_1,S_2\). Giving each of these sets weight \(1/2\) is therefore a fractional coloring of total weight \(3/2\). The digraph contains an arc, so Proposition~\ref{prop:lower} proves equality.

\needspace{5\baselineskip}
For the second assertion, let $K=\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(D_2(\mathcal I))$. We have \(K\geqslant3/2\) by Proposition~\ref{prop:lower}. Lemma~\ref{lem:distribution} gives a random majority-stable set \(S\) with every inclusion probability exactly \(1/K\). Put \(J=V(D_2)\setminus S\). Every vertex is omitted with probability \(1-1/K\). Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tau}
\tau=3\left(1-\frac1K\right)-1=2-\frac3K.
\end{equation}
For every variable \(v\), let \(L_v=\{i\in\mathbb Z_3:x_{v,i}\in J\}\). This list is nonempty in every outcome: if it were empty, \(S\) would contain \(x_{v,0}\) and both of its outneighbors, contradicting majority stability. Exact marginals give \(\mathbb E|L_v|=3(1-1/K)=1+\tau\), hence \(\mathbb E(|L_v|-1)=\tau\). Thus \(\tau\) is the expected number of extra available labels beyond the one that every variable must have. In particular, when \(K=3/2\), all lists are singletons almost surely. When \(K\) is close to \(3/2\), the expected number of extra labels is small.

Sample \(J\), and then, conditional on \(J\), choose a label \(a(v)\) uniformly from \(L_v\), independently for different variables. We do not assume that the lists, or the membership indicators of \(J\), are independent. For a constraint \(e=(u,v,c_e)\), write \(L_v+c_e=\{j+c_e:j\in L_v\}\). Because \(u\ne v\), the two final choices \(a(u)\) and \(a(v)+c_e\) are conditionally independent and uniform on \(L_u\) and \(L_v+c_e\). Of the \(|L_u||L_v|\) equally likely ordered pairs, precisely \(|L_u\cap(L_v+c_e)|\) have equal coordinates. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:listviolation}
\mathbb P\bigl(a(u)-a(v)=c_e\mid J\bigr)
=\frac{|L_u\cap(L_v+c_e)|}{|L_u||L_v|}.
\end{equation}

To bound the numerator, fix a label \(i\in\mathbb Z_3\) and consider the triple
\(\{x_{u,i},x_{v,i-c_e},z_{e,i}\}\).
At least one of these vertices is omitted: otherwise \(z_{e,i}\in S\) would have both outneighbors in \(S\). Thus the number of omitted vertices in this triple, minus one, is nonnegative. Moreover, if \(i\in L_u\cap(L_v+c_e)\), both variable vertices of the triple are omitted, so this number is at least one. Summing these pointwise observations over the three labels gives
\[
|L_u\cap(L_v+c_e)|
\leqslant\sum_{i\in\mathbb Z_3}
\left(|J\cap\{x_{u,i},x_{v,i-c_e},z_{e,i}\}|-1\right).
\]
Each triple has three distinct vertices, each omitted with probability \(1-1/K\). By linearity of expectation, the expected value of each summand on the right is \(3(1-1/K)-1=\tau\). Independence is not needed. Hence
\(\mathbb E|L_u\cap(L_v+c_e)|\leqslant3\tau\).
Since both lists are nonempty, their product of sizes is at least one. Taking expectations in~\eqref{eq:listviolation} now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P\bigl(a(u)-a(v)=c_e\bigr)
&=\mathbb E\left[\frac{|L_u\cap(L_v+c_e)|}{|L_u||L_v|}\right]\\
&\leqslant\mathbb E|L_u\cap(L_v+c_e)|\leqslant3\tau.
\end{aligned}
\]
Multiplying the inequality for constraint \(e\) by its weight \(w_e\), summing over all constraints, and using \(\sum_e w_e=1\), we obtain
\[
\mathbb E\left[\sum_{e=(u,v,c_e)}w_e\mathbf1_{\{a(u)-a(v)=c_e\}}\right]
=\sum_{e=(u,v,c_e)}w_e\mathbb P\bigl(a(u)-a(v)=c_e\bigr)
\leqslant3\tau.
\]
At least one assignment has total violated weight no greater than this expectation. By the definition of \(\mu\), we conclude that \(\mu(\mathcal I)\leqslant3\tau=6-9/K\). Consequently \(9/K\leqslant6-\mu(\mathcal I)\); the right-hand side is positive since \(0\leqslant\mu(\mathcal I)\leqslant1\). Rearranging proves~\eqref{eq:D2soundness}.

label: cor:threehalves
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:threehalves}
Deciding whether a digraph $D$ satisfies $\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(D)=3/2$ is NP-complete, even for acyclic oriented digraphs with outdegrees zero or two in which every directed path has length at most two.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: NP-hardness follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:D2} and the source hardness theorem. For membership in NP, reject edgeless inputs; otherwise Proposition~\ref{prop:lower} gives $\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(D)\geqslant3/2$. The covering LP~\eqref{eq:lp} has a basic optimal solution with at most $|V(D)|$ positive weights, all rational and of polynomial bit length. A family of majority-stable sets with these weights and total weight at most $3/2$ is therefore a polynomial certificate: majority stability, vertex coverage and total weight can all be checked in polynomial time.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:D2} maps a satisfiable source instance to value \(a=3/2\), and a NO instance with \(\mu(\mathcal I)>1/12-\eta\) to a value greater than \(108/(71+12\eta)\). Thus, for every fixed \(\beta\) with \(a<\beta<B:=108/71\), choosing a sufficiently small fixed \(\eta>0\) gives NP-hardness of distinguishing value \(a\) from a value greater than \(\beta\), on acyclic oriented digraphs of maximum outdegree two.

A multiplicative approximation of ratio \(\rho<B/a=72/71\) would separate these cases: choose \(\rho a<\beta<B\), so its output is at most \(\rho a\) in the YES case and greater than \(\beta\) in the NO case. Likewise, for an additive upper estimate with error \(\delta<B-a=3/142\), choose \(a+\delta<\beta<B\); its output is then at most \(a+\delta\) in the YES case and greater than \(\beta\) in the NO case. In either case a fixed rational threshold between the two output ranges would solve the NP-hard promise problem in polynomial time.

title: Proof
body_md:
The empty tournament has value zero, so assume \(T\) is nonempty. Write \(s=|K|\). The strong components of a tournament are linearly ordered, with every arc between two components pointing in the same direction. Thus every vertex outside \(K\) dominates every vertex in \(K\), and the outdegrees of vertices in \(K\) equal their outdegrees within \(K\).

Every \(z\in K\) can be the last vertex of a directed Hamilton path of \(T\): indeed, the subtournament outside \(K\) has a Hamilton path, possibly empty. If \(K\) is a singleton, append it. Otherwise, there exists a Hamilton cycle in \(K\), break its outgoing arc at \(z\) to obtain a Hamilton path ending at \(z\), and append this path to the one outside \(K\).

There are exactly \(\binom{s}{2}\) arcs inside \(K\), and none leaving \(K\). Consequently \(\sum_{v\in K}(2d(v)+1)=2\binom{s}{2}+s=s^2\). Apply Cauchy--Schwarz to the vectors with coordinates \(\sqrt{2d(v)+1}\) and \(1/\sqrt{2d(v)+1}\). It gives
\[
s^2=\left(\sum_{v\in K}\sqrt{2d(v)+1}\,
\frac1{\sqrt{2d(v)+1}}\right)^2
\leqslant\left(\sum_{v\in K}(2d(v)+1)\right)
\left(\sum_{v\in K}\frac1{2d(v)+1}\right)
=s^2Z.
\]
Since \(s>0\), this proves \(Z\geqslant1\).

Let \(r_v\) denote the probability that \(v\) is chosen as the endpoint: \(r_v=1/(Z(2d(v)+1))\) for \(v\in K\), and \(r_v=0\) otherwise. Thus \(r_v\leqslant1/(2d(v)+1)\) for every vertex. For a fixed choice of the endpoint, a vertex distinct from it is a designated matched tail with probability \(1/2\), while the endpoint never is. The protection event \(P_v\) has probability \(q_v=(1-r_v)/2\).

For a vertex of outdegree \(d\geqslant1\), we therefore have
\(q_v\geqslant(1-1/(2d+1))/2=d/(2d+1)\).
Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:survival} with this protection guarantee gives \(\mathbb P(v\in S_0)\geqslant h_d:= L_d\left(\frac{d}{2d+1}\right) \). A sink is never deleted and survives with probability \(b=4/9\).

It remains to minimize \(h_d\). The even-degree comparison in Section~\ref{sec:degreemin} gives \(L_{2m}(q)\geqslant L_{2m-1}(q)\), and \(L_d(q)\) is nondecreasing in \(q\). Since \(2m/(4m+1)\geqslant(2m-1)/(4m-1)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_{2m}=L_{2m}\left(\frac{2m}{4m+1}\right)
&\geqslant L_{2m-1}\left(\frac{2m}{4m+1}\right)\\
&\geqslant L_{2m-1}\left(\frac{2m-1}{4m-1}\right)=h_{2m-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
It is therefore enough to compare odd degrees.

Recall \(R_j=\binom{2j}{j}(20/81)^j\) and \(\Phi_d(b)=\mathbb P(\operatorname{Bin}(d,b)>d/2)\), with \(b=4/9\). Applying~\eqref{eq:Lodd} with \(q=(2j+1)/(4j+3)\) gives
\[
h_{2j+1}=b(1-\Phi_{2j+1}(b))+b^2\frac{2j+1}{4j+3}R_j.
\]
For \(m\geqslant1\), subtracting the expressions for consecutive odd degrees and using~\eqref{eq:binomialdifference} together with
\(R_m=\frac{40(2m-1)}{81m}R_{m-1}\) gives
\[
h_{2m+1}-h_{2m-1}
=R_{m-1}\frac{16(2m-1)(76m^2-123m-55)}{6561m(4m+3)(4m-1)}.
\]
Every factor except the quadratic is positive. Moreover, $76m^2-123m-55=3+(m-2)(76m+29)$, which is
\(-102\) at \(m=1\), while
it is positive, for $m\geqslant 2$.
Thus \(h_3<h_1\), and the odd-degree values increase strictly from
degree three onwards. Together with the even-degree comparison,
this proves that \(h_d\geqslant h_3\) for every \(d\geqslant1\).

Finally, the definition~\eqref{eq:Ldq} gives, at \(b=4/9\),
\[
h_3=L_3(3/7)
=b\left[\frac47\bigl((1-b)^3+3b(1-b)^2\bigr)
+\frac37(1-b^2)\right]
=\frac{13820}{45927}.
\]
The sink probability \(4/9\) is larger. Every vertex therefore belongs to \(S_0\) with probability at least \(13820/45927\), and Lemma~\ref{lem:distribution} gives \(\chi^*_{\mathrm{maj}}(T)\leqslant45927/13820<3.324\).
